title: Caps, cans, and the triangle
description: Ten short reads on what belongs with what. Two harder ones at the end.

questions.question: These stiff, cloudy bottles sit together. What family are they?
options: HDPE — detergent, dairy, and many kitchen jugs
PET — the same as clear water bottles
Glass with a plastic skin
Film, because they held liquid
questions.answer: HDPE — detergent, dairy, and many kitchen jugs
questions.explanation: Stiff and cloudy is the HDPE look. Clear crackly water bottles are PET. Keep the families apart.

questions.question: Hands are gathering bottle caps in their own pile. Why not leave them on the bottles?
options: The cap is usually a different grade from the bottle
Caps make the bottle worth more as one piece
Caps are glass
Caps dissolve if you leave them on
questions.answer: The cap is usually a different grade from the bottle
questions.explanation: Most drink bottles are PET. Most caps are PP or HDPE. Unscrewing is the sort.

questions.question: This tub flexes and goes pale at the bend. Which quiet grade is that often?
options: PP — many yoghurt cups and kitchen tubs
PET — it must be a water bottle
Film — it held food
Metal — pale means aluminium
questions.answer: PP — many yoghurt cups and kitchen tubs
questions.explanation: PP is the waxed, flex-and-white cup. It is not PET and it is not a bag.

questions.question: A milk-style bottle, opaque, not see-through. First guess?
options: HDPE, unless the triangle says otherwise
Always PET, because it held a drink
Always glass
Always film
questions.answer: HDPE, unless the triangle says otherwise
questions.explanation: Household milk and many juice jugs are HDPE. Still turn it over if you can.

questions.question: Clear, green, and brown bottles share one mesh cage. What makes that cage a product?
options: They are all PET bottles kept as one grade
Colour mixing means three different grades
The cage turns them into HDPE
Mesh means they are residual only
questions.answer: They are all PET bottles kept as one grade
questions.explanation: PET can be several colours and still be PET. Grade first, colour second.

questions.question: Thin bags hang in riverside branches. What is the household move?
options: Keep film in a tied sack so wind cannot take it
Stuff the bags inside PET bottles to hide them
Burn the bags with the supper fire
Leave them — film cannot travel
questions.answer: Keep film in a tied sack so wind cannot take it
questions.explanation: Film flies. A tied sack is the sort. Bottles and fire are the wrong rooms.

questions.question: Bottles float in a river beside houses. If nobody lifts them, where do they ride?
options: Toward the sea — rivers are the road
They become soil in a week
They stay in that bend forever
Rain dissolves them
questions.answer: Toward the sea — rivers are the road
questions.explanation: Most ocean plastic started inland. Catch it dry at the house.

questions.question: A yard door is a mixed heap of bags, bottles, and film. Why is that heap expensive?
options: Every grade must be pulled apart again before a sale
Mixed plastic always sells for more
It can be melted as one material
Mixed heaps are burned, so sorting is pointless
questions.answer: Every grade must be pulled apart again before a sale
questions.explanation: A buyer wants one grade. Mixing is unpaid work for the next pair of hands.

questions.question: Blue jerry cans are banded in one bale, white in another. Why split colour?
options: Same grade, one colour, a pellet a buyer can trust
Blue plastic is a different grade from white
Bands only hold on matching colours
Colour is just for the photo
questions.answer: Same grade, one colour, a pellet a buyer can trust
questions.explanation: Grade first, colour second. Mixed colours melt muddy.

questions.question: Lentil-sized beads in grass, not broken bottles. What are they?
options: Nurdles — raw pellets spilled before anything was made
Seeds that only grow near plastic
Finished household recycled cups
Bleached sand
questions.answer: Nurdles — raw pellets spilled before anything was made
questions.explanation: Nurdles are plastic at the start of its life. Once loose, they are almost impossible to gather.
